DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Pattern Discovery 
❑ Pattern
▪ A set of items, subsequences, or substructures that occur frequently together in a data set
▪ Patterns represent intrinsic and important properties of data sets

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Pattern Discovery 
❑ Pattern discovery
▪ Uncovering patterns from massive data sets
▪ It can answer questions such as:
• What products were often purchased together?
• What are the subsequent purchases after buying an iPad?
• What are the frequent communication patterns in social network services?
❑ Foundation for many essential data science tasks
▪ Association, correlation, and causality analysis
▪ Discriminative pattern-based classification
▪ Pattern-based subspace clustering
7
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Pattern Discovery 
❑ Broad applications
▪ Market basket analysis, cross-marketing, catalog design, sale campaign analysis, Web log 
analysis, biological sequence analysis
▪ Many types of data: transactions, graph, spatiotemporal, time-series, and stream data

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Frequent Itemsets
11
❑ Support s(X) of an itemset X
▪ Absolute support → count
• The occurrences of an itemset in all transactions
• e.g., s({Beer}) = 3, s({Diaper}) = 4, s({Beer, Eggs}) = 1
‒ Can be also written as {Beer}:3 for simplicity
▪ Relative support → ratio
• The fraction of transactions that contain X
• i.e., the probability that a transaction contains X
• e.g., s({Beer}) = 3/5 = 60%, s({Diaper}) = 4/5 = 80%, s({Beer, Eggs}) = 1/5 = 20%
‒ Can be also written as {Beer}:60% or {Beer}:0.6
▪ They can be used interchangeably 
• e.g., given 10 transactions, the absolute support for an itemset is 3 → the relative support 30% = 0.3

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Frequent Itemsets
❑ Frequent itemsets
▪ An itemset X is frequent if s(X) is no less than a minsup (minimum support threshold) 
• i.e., s(X) ≥ minsup
▪ e.g., given 5 transactions and a minsup = 50% (= 5*0.5 = 2.5)
• Frequent 1-itemsets
‒ e.g., Beer: 3/5 (= 60%)
‒ What about Milk?
• Frequent 2-itemsets
‒ e.g., {Beer, Diaper}: 3/5 (= 60%)
‒ What about {Beer, Nuts}?
• Frequent 3-itemsets
‒ Is there any?

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Association Rule
❑ Association rule
▪ Given itemsets X and Y, X → Y
• i.e., if X, then Y: when X occurs, then Y will as well
❑ The strength of an association rule
▪ Support of X∪Y (i.e., s(X∪Y))
• e.g., s({Diaper, Beer}) = 3/5 = 60%
▪ Confidence of X→Y (i.e., c(X→Y))
• The conditional probability that a transaction containing X also contains Y
‒ c(X→Y) =s(X⋃Y)
s(X)
• e.g., the confidence of a rule Diaper → Beer?
‒ c(Diaper→Beer) = s({Diaper, Beer})
s({Diaper}) =
3
4 = 0.75
• e.g., the confidence of a rule Beer → Diaper?
‒ c(Beer →Diaper) = s({Diaper, Beer})
s({Beer}) =
3
3 = 1.0

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Association Rule
❑ RECAP: frequent itemsets and association rule
▪ An itemset X is frequent if s(X) is no less than minsup (minimum support) 
• i.e., s(X) ≥ minsup
▪ An association rule X→Y is confident if c(X→Y) is no less than minconf (minimum confidence)
• i.e., c(X→Y) ≥ minconf
▪ e.g., given a minsup = 50% and minconf = 80%
• Frequent itemsets
‒ Beer: 3/5 (= 60%); Nuts: 3/5 (= 60%); Diaper: 4/5 (= 80%); 
 Eggs: 3/5 (= 60%), {Beer, Diaper}: 3/5 (= 60%)
• Confident (strong) association rules
‒ Beer → Diaper: c(Beer→Diaper) = 1 (= 100%)
‒ Diaper → Beer: c(Diaper→Beer) = 0.75 (= 75%) 
❑ Mining frequent itemsets and association rules are very close problems
▪ Can we think of scalable methods for large datasets?
▪ Can we think of minimum but still sufficient information for identifying them?

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Closed and Maximal Patterns
❑ Expressing patterns in compressed forms
▪ Closed patterns
• A frequent pattern (itemset) X is closed if X is frequent (i.e., s(X) ≥ minsup), and there 
exists no super-itemset with the same support (i.e., for all Y⊃X, s(Y) ≠ s(X) or s(Y) < s(X))
‒ e.g., if minsup = 1, closed patterns will be “{a1, …, a50}: 2” and “{a1, …, a100}: 1” 
• Closed patterns are lossless compression of frequent patterns 
‒ Reduce the number of patterns without losing support information
‒ i.e., it is possible to exactly know the support of any frequent patterns in the closed patterns
‒ e.g., {a2, …, a49}: 2, {a5, a99}: 1, …

Closed 
Patterns
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Closed and Maximal Patterns
❑ Expressing patterns in compressed forms
▪ Maximal patterns
• A frequent pattern (itemset) X is maximal if X is frequent (i.e., s(X) ≥ minsup), and there 
exists no frequent super-itemset Y⊃X (i.e, for all Y⊃X, s(Y) < minsup)
‒ e.g., if minsup = 1, maximal patterns will be “{a1, …, a100}: 1” 
‒ What about  “{a1, …, a50}: 2”? There exists a frequent super-itemset  “{a1, …, a100} ⊃ {a1, …, a50}”  
• Maximal patterns are lossy compression of frequent patterns
‒ Reduce the number of patterns but lose support information
‒ i.e., we do not exactly know the support of any frequent patterns in the maximal patterns
‒ e.g., We know that {a1, …, a40} is frequent, but do not know its support (which is 2)

▪ We can compress patterns without losing support information

DAIS lab at Korea University
Frequent, Closed, Maximal Patterns (Itemsets)
❑ k-itemset X
▪ An itemset including k items
▪ k can be from one to the number of unique items
❑ Frequent itemsets FX
▪ k-itemsets whose supports are no less than the minsup threshold
▪ s(X) ≥ minsup
❑ Closed frequent itemsets CX
▪ Frequent itemsets with no super-itemset of the same support
▪ s(CX) ≥ minsup & for all Y⊃CX, s(Y) ≠ s(CX)
▪ Adding any other item to a closed frequent itemset changes its support
❑ Maximal frequent itemsets MX
▪ Frequent itemsets with no frequent super-itemset
▪ s(MX) ≥ minsup & for all Y⊃MX, s(Y) < minsup
▪ Adding any other item to a maximal frequent itemset makes it infrequent
All itemsets
{Beer}:3, {Diaper}:3, {Eggs}:3, {Coffee}:2,
{Beer, Diaper}:2, {Beer, Coffee}:1, {Beer, Eggs}:1, 
{Diaper, Coffee}:1, {Diaper, Eggs}:2, {Coffee, Eggs}:1,
 {Beer, Diaper, Coffee}:0, {Beer, Diaper, Eggs}:1, 
{Beer, Coffee, Eggs}:0, {Diaper, Coffee, Eggs}:1
{Beer, Diaper, Eggs, Coffee}:0

Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Discovery
❑ Given a set of transactions, we want to find all rules X → Y where 
▪ Support s(X∪Y) ≥ minsup threshold
▪ Confidence c(X→Y) = s(X∪Y)/s(X) ≥ minconf threshold
❑ Example
▪ Association rule: Beer → Diaper ?

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Discovery
❑ Brute-force approach 1
▪ Procedure
• Step 1: From the unique items, list all possible association rules
• Step 2: Compute the support and confidence for each rule
• Step 3: Prune rules with the minsup and minconf thresholds
▪ Issue: computationally prohibitive!
• Given d unique items, the number of rules

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Discovery
❑ Brute-force approach 2
▪ Procedure
• Step 1: Find frequent itemsets (minsup)
‒ From the unique items, generate all possible itemsets 
‒ Compute the support and prune by the minsup threshold
• Step 2: Find association rules (minconf)
‒ From the frequent itemsets, generate all possible association rules
‒ Compute the confidence and prune by the minconf threshold
▪ Issue: step 1 is still computationally expensive!
• Given d unique items, 
‒ The number of transactions: N
‒ The number of items in transactions: W
‒ The number of itemsets: M = 2d
• The computational complexity ~ O(NWM)
‒ For each of N transactions with W items, check against M itemsets

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Discovery
❑ Strategies for finding frequent itemsets
▪ Reduce the number of transactions (N)
• Reduce the size of N as the size of itemset increases
• e.g., Partitioning, vertical-data format (i.e., item → TIDs)
▪ Reduce the number of candidates (M)
• Use pruning techniques to reduce M
• e.g., Apriori
▪ Reduce the number of comparisons (N x M)
• Use efficient data structures (e.g., hash tables) to store the 
candidates or transactions
• No need to match every candidate against every transaction
• e.g., Dynamic hashing and pruning, FP-growth

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Apriori
❑ Revisiting the extreme cases
▪ Suppose that we have minsup = 2
▪ We have a closed and maximal frequent itemset: {a1, …, a50}:2
▪ What are the supports of {a1}, {a2}, …, {a50}, {a1, a2}, …, {a1, …, a49}, …?
▪ Can we guarantee that all subsets of {a1, …, a50} are frequent?
▪ Can we guarantee that these are all frequent itemsets?

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Apriori
❑ Observation
▪ All items in an itemset X should be in its superset Y
• e.g., every transaction containing Y = {Beer, Diaper, Nuts} also contains X = {Beer, Diaper} 
▪ The support of an itemset X is larger than or equal to the support of its superset Y 
• i.e., ∀𝑿, 𝒀: 𝑿 ⊆ 𝒀 , 𝒔(𝑿) ≥ 𝒔(𝒀) a.k.a. anti-monotone property of support

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Apriori
❑ Observation
▪ All items in an itemset X should be in its superset Y
• e.g., every transaction containing Y = {Beer, Diaper, Nuts} also contains X = {Beer, Diaper} 
▪ The support of an itemset X is larger than or equal to the support of its superset Y 
• i.e., ∀𝑿, 𝒀: 𝑿 ⊆ 𝒀 , 𝒔(𝑿) ≥ 𝒔(𝒀) a.k.a. anti-monotone property of support
❑ The downward closure (a.k.a. “Apriori”) property of frequent patterns
▪ Apriori: a Latin phrase that means "from what is earlier"
▪ If an itemset Y is frequent, then all of its subsets X must also be frequent
• i.e., ∀𝑋, 𝑌: 𝑋 ⊆ 𝑌 , 𝑠(𝑌) ≥ minsup → 𝑠(𝑋) ≥ minsup
▪ In other words, if an itemset X is not frequent, any superset Y of it can not be frequent
• i.e., ∀𝑋, 𝑌: 𝑋 ⊆ 𝑌 , 𝑠 𝑋 < minsup → 𝑠 𝑌 < minsup
38
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Apriori
❑ Example usage of the apriori property of frequent patterns
▪ If an itemset {A, B} is infrequent, should we check all of its super-itemsets?

40
❑ The Apriori algorithm
▪ Basic idea
• From k=1, incrementally generate candidate itemsets and find frequent itemsets by scanning TDB
‒ i.e., if k-itemset is frequent, (k+1)-itemset can be frequent
▪ Overall procedure for finding frequent itemsets
Ck: Candidate itemset of size k
Fk : Frequent itemset of size k
k := 1;
Fk := {frequent items};   // Frequent 1-itemset
While (Fk != ) do {  // When Fk is non-empty
    Ck+1 := candidates generated from Fk;  // candidate generation
    Derive Fk+1 by counting candidates in Ck+1 in TDB and compare with minsup;
    k := k + 1
   }
return k Fk    // Return Fk generated at each level

❑ Pseudo-code of Apriori for finding frequent itemsets

❑ Motivation
▪ In TDB, let X be a frequent itemset, TDB’ be the set of transactions that contain X
▪ If a new item y is a frequent item in TDB’, then {y}∪X must be a frequent itemset

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ Motivation
▪ In TDB, let X be a frequent itemset, TDB’ be the set of transactions that contain X
▪ If a new item y is a frequent item in TDB’, then {y}∪X must be a frequent itemset
❑ FP-Growth (frequent pattern growth)
▪ Main idea
• A compact data structure FP-tree is constructed to store information for finding frequent patterns
• Recursively find frequent itemsets from FP-tree
▪ Advantages
• No candidate itemsets generation is required (unlike Apriori)
• Scan TDB only twice!
60
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ The FP-Growth algorithm for finding frequent patterns
▪ Input: a transactional database TDB, minsup
▪ Procedures
1. Find frequent 1-itemsets (1st TDB scan)
‒ e.g., minsup = 60% (=3) → f:4, c:4, a:3, b:3, m:3, p:3

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ The FP-Growth algorithm for finding frequent patterns
▪ Input: a transactional database TDB, minsup
▪ Procedures
1. Find frequent 1-itemsets (1st TDB scan)
‒ e.g., minsup = 60% (=3) → f:4, c:4, a:3, b:3, m:3, p:3
2. Build f-lists
‒ For each transactions, sort the frequent items by frequency to get a f-list
‒ e.g., {f, a, c, d, g, i, m, p} → f, c, a, m, p

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ The FP-Growth algorithm for finding frequent patterns
▪ Input: a transactional database TDB, minsup
▪ Procedures
1. Find frequent 1-itemsets (1st TDB scan)
2. Build f-lists
3. Construct FP-tree (2nd TDB scan)
4. Find frequent itemsets with FP-tree

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ FP-Growth Step 4.1: form conditional pattern bases: pattern_base | α
▪ A partition of frequent patterns
• A sub TDB which consists of the set of prefix paths in the FP-tree 
    with a frequent itemset α as a co-occurring suffix pattern
▪ e.g., α = {m}
• conditional pattern bases | {m} = {f,c,a}:2, {f,c,a,b}:1
‒ i.e., {f, c, a}: support = 2 and {f, c, a, b}: support = 1

❑ FP-Growth Step 4.2: construct conditional FP-trees: FP-tree |  α
▪ A small FP-tree on the conditional pattern base pattern_base | α
▪ e.g., α = {m}
• Conditional pattern bases | {m} = {f, c, a}:2, {f, c, a, b}:1
• Conditional FP-tree | {m} = f:3 – c:3 – a:3
‒ A conditional FP-tree with the given minsup =  3
‒ b:1 < minsup = 3 is not included in the conditional FP-tree

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ FP-Growth Step 4.3: recursively find frequent k-itemsets (k>1)
▪ Recursively construct conditional FP-tree | α and find frequent itemsets
▪ e.g., α = {m}
→ Conditional pattern bases | {m} = {f, c, a}:2, {f, c, a, b}:1
→ Conditional FP-tree | {m} = f:3 – c:3 – a:3 
→ Frequent 2-itemset: {a, m}, {c, m}, {f, m}
→  Conditional pattern bases | {a, m} = {f, c}: 3
→  Conditional FP-tree | {a, m} = f:3 – c:3
 → Frequent 3-itemset: {c, a, m}, {f, a, m}
  → Conditional pattern bases | {c, a, m} = {f}:3
  → Conditional FP-tree | {c, a, m} = f:3
  → Frequent 4-itemset: {f, c, a, m}
→ Conditional pattern bases | {c, m} = {f}:3
 → Conditional FP-tree | {c, m} = f:3
 → Frequent 3-itemset: {f, c, m}

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > FP-Growth 
❑ Recap of FP-Growth
▪ Find frequent 1-itemsets (1st scan) 
▪ Construct a customized data structure, FP-tree (2nd scan)
▪ For each frequent 1-itemset, 
• Partition the TDB based on them (i.e., conditional pattern base)
• Recursively exploit FP-tree (i.e., conditional FP-tree) to grow frequent patterns from each partition
• Stop conditions
‒ The resulting FP-tree is empty (e.g., FP-tree | {f}))
 → No further pattern base exists
‒ The resulting FP-tree contains only one path (e.g., FP-tree | {m})
→ All the combinations of its sub-paths become frequent patterns

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Generation
❑ Given a frequent itemset X, 
▪ Possible association rules
• All non-empty subsets Y ⊂ X such that X-Y → Y satisfies the minimum confidence threshold
• If |X| = k, then there are 2k – 2 candidate association rules (except for X →  and  → X)
▪ Example
• If X = {A,B,C,D} is a frequent itemset, candidate rules can be:
85
BCD→A ACD→B ABD→C ABC→D
CD→AB BD→AC BC→AD AD→BC AC→BD AB→CD
D→ABC C→ABD B→ACD A→BCD
{  }
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Generation
86
❑ How to efficiently generate rules from frequent itemsets?
▪ Unlike support, confidence does not have an anti-monotone property
▪ Example X = {A, B, D} ⊆ Y = {A, B, C, D}
• Support
‒ s({A, B, D}) ≥ s({A, B, C, D})
• Confidence 
‒ Frequent 4-itemset {A, B, C, D}: c(ABC → D) = s({A,B,C,D})/s({A,B,C} 
‒ Frequent 3-itemset {A, B, D}: c(AB → D) = s({A,B,D})/s({A,B} 
‒ c(ABC → D) ?? c(AB → D)
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Methodologies > Rule Generation
87
❑ How to efficiently generate rules from frequent itemsets?
▪ Confidence does not have an anti-monotone property
• e.g., c(ABC → D) can be larger or smaller than c(AB → D)
▪ Confidence of rules generated from the same itemset has an anti-monotone property
• Confidence is anti-monotone w.r.t. the number of items on the right-hand-side of the rule
• e.g., X = {A,B,C,D}: c(BCD → A) ≥ c(CD → AB) ≥ c(D → ABC)
BCD→A ACD→B ABD→C ABC→D
CD→AB BD→AC BC→AD AD→BC AC→BD AB→CD
D→ABC C→ABD B→ACD A→BCD
{  }

DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Evaluation > Motivation
❑ Are support and confidence sufficient? 
▪ Example
• TDB with minsup = 30% and minconf = 60%
‒ Total 10,000 transactions
‒ 6,000 transactions include “game”
‒ 7,500 transactions include “video”
‒ 4,000 transactions include both “game” and “video”
• A strong rule discovered: {“game”} → {“video”} 
‒ Support = 4,000/10,000 = 40% > minsup
‒ Confidence = 4,000/6,000 = 66% > minconf
• Is it interesting?
‒ It can be misleading because the probability of purchasing “video” is 7,500/10,000 = 75% > 66%
89
DAIS lab at Korea University
Pattern Mining > Evaluation > Lift
❑ Correlation measure: Lift
▪ The degree to which the occurrence of one “lifts” the occurrence of the other
• 𝑃 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 = 𝑃 𝐴 × 𝑃 𝐵  → Lift = 1: A and B are independent
• 𝑃 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 > 𝑃 𝐴 × 𝑃 𝐵  → Lift > 1: A and B are positively correlated
• 𝑃 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 < 𝑃 𝐴 × 𝑃 𝐵  → Lift < 1: A and B are negatively correlated
▪ Example
• Lift(game, video) = 0.4/(0.6 x 0.75) = 0.89 < 1
• The sale of game is said to increase the likelihood of the sale of video by a factor of lift = 0.89
‒ Negatively correlated → the sale of game does not help the sale of video 
▪ It is more informative if we have the lift score in addition to the support and confidence
‒ “A → B” [support, confidence, lift]
90
𝑙𝑖𝑓𝑡 𝐴, 𝐵 = 𝑐 𝐴 → 𝐵
𝑠 𝐵 = 𝑠 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵
𝑠 𝐴 × 𝑠 𝐵 = 𝑃 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵
𝑃 𝐴 × 𝑃 𝐵
